prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN)  -- Charging chesty women more for their bras doesn't win a lot of support, British retailer Marks & Spencer acknowledged Friday as it announced an end to the surcharge on its larger lingerie. Marks & Spencer have apologised for charging chesty women more for bras. "We boobed," screamed a full-page Marks & Spencer ad, which appeared in British newspapers Friday. Marks & Spencer gave in to campaigners who argued that the higher prices of the bigger bras was unfair. The retailer charged as much as £2 ($3) more for all sizes DD and up. "It's true that our fantastic quality larger bras cost more money to make, and we felt it was right to reflect this in the prices we charged," the ad said. "Well, we were wrong." It follows a nearly year-long campaign by members of the Facebook group Busts 4 Justice. The women behind the site argued other chain retailers didn't charge extra for bigger sizes, so Marks & Spencer shouldn't, either. And it pointed out that the store doesn't charge extra for larger sizes of clothing, so it shouldn't charge more for larger undergarments. What's your view? "We would like to thank everyone who has supported us on this issue; especially the thousands of brilliant, busty women that have joined forces with us. We couldn't have done this without you," the two administrators of the group, Becky Mount and Beckie Williams, posted Friday on Facebook. "Busts 4 Justice remain committed to making things better for busty women on the high street, but for now we're happy just to be able to encourage all ladies to reward themselves and their boobs with some properly fitted, fairly priced lingerie." Marks & Spencer is a stalwart British chain, known for classic wardrobe staples and low prices. Its underwear department is the first stop for many British shoppers and is especially famous for reliable basics. And to give customers an added lift, Marks & Spencer also announced it is cutting the prices of all of its bras by 25 percent for the rest of May. "I think even though we all obviously held a bit of a grudge against buying our bras from M&S we should really be grateful they got rid of the surcharge and have given us the super generous 25 percent off," Mount wrote on the group's site Friday. "They may get cleared out by the time the weekend is over!"

“Busts 4 Justice remain committed to making things better for busty women on the high street, but for now we’re happy just to be able to encourage all ladies to reward themselves and their boobs with some properly fitted, fairly priced lingerie.”

Marks & Spencer is a longstanding British chain, known for classic wardrobe staples and affordable prices. Its underwear department is the first destination for many British shoppers and is especially well known for dependable basics.

In a further boost for customers, Marks & Spencer also announced that it would reduce the prices of all its bras by 25 percent for the remainder of May.

“I think even though we all obviously held a bit of a grudge against buying our bras from M&S we should really be grateful they got rid of the surcharge and have given us the super generous 25 percent off,” Mount wrote on the group’s site Friday. “They may get cleared out by the time the weekend is over!”

**Marks & Spencer drops extra charge for larger bras after Facebook campaign**

*By [Staff Writer], CNN-style report*

Marks & Spencer has announced it will stop charging extra for larger bra sizes following a highly visible online campaign by a customer group calling itself **Busts 4 Justice**.

The British retailer had faced criticism for adding an extra charge — reportedly around £2 — to bras in larger cup sizes, a policy campaigners dubbed unfair to women with bigger busts. The issue gained momentum after Busts 4 Justice launched a Facebook campaign accusing the company of imposing what supporters described as a “boob tax.”

Marks & Spencer initially defended the pricing, saying larger bras required more fabric and additional design work to provide proper support. But after thousands of customers joined the online protest and media attention grew, the retailer reversed course.

The company said it would now apply one price across bra sizes in the same range, ending the surcharge on larger cups. Marks & Spencer also apologized to customers who felt singled out by the policy.

Campaigners welcomed the decision as a victory for consumers and for online activism.

Busts 4 Justice said the response showed that customers could use social media to hold major retailers accountable. The group argued that women should not be penalized for needing a larger size, particularly for an everyday clothing item.

The change marked a notable climbdown for Marks & Spencer, one of the United Kingdom’s best-known lingerie retailers, and underscored the growing influence of Facebook-based consumer campaigns in pressuring companies to rethink pricing policies.
